title: Italy Turn to Pirlo After Ancelotti, Guardiola Reject Azzurri Job
excerpt: The Italian Football Federation is poised to appoint the former Juventus midfielder as head coach after both Carlo Ancelotti and Pep Guardiola declined the role, with an official announcement expected this weekend.
body:
• Italy's FIGC first approached Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti, then Pep Guardiola, but both declined the vacant national team coaching role.
  • Guardiola wanted €20 million per year — double the FIGC's budget — and has opted for an extended break from management after leaving Manchester City in May.
  • Andrea Pirlo, 47, is now the overwhelming favourite and could be announced before the end of the weekend, earning around €1.5 million annually.
  • Technical director Paolo Maldini and advisor Leonardo are steering a long-term rebuild after Italy's failure to qualify for a third consecutive World Cup.

Italy are closing in on Andrea Pirlo as their next head coach after both Carlo Ancelotti and Pep Guardiola turned down the chance to revive the four-time world champions, according to journalist Matteo Moretto.

An official announcement is expected before the end of the weekend, ending a turbulent search that began when Gennaro Gattuso stepped down in April following Italy's failure to qualify for a third straight World Cup.

The Search for a Supercoach

New FIGC president Giovanni Malago tasked Paolo Maldini, recently installed as technical director, with rebuilding the Azzurri from the ground up. Maldini, aided by former Paris Saint-Germain sporting director Leonardo, aimed high.

https://x.com/433/status/2080644837213134989

"We cannot deny that we also spoke to Carlo Ancelotti before talking to Pep, and it felt only right to start with those we considered to be the best in the world."

— Paolo Maldini, FIGC Technical Director

Ancelotti, 67, was the first call. The former AC Milan and Real Madrid manager — Maldini's old teammate — is under contract with Brazil through the 2030 World Cup. Despite a disappointing round-of-16 exit to Norway at the 2026 tournament, Ancelotti has committed to staying with the Seleção, according to transfer specialist Fabrizio Romano. The Brazilian Football Confederation confirmed he would remain in charge.

Guardiola Says No

With Ancelotti off the table, Maldini and Leonardo flew to Barcelona last weekend to make their pitch to Guardiola in person. The Spaniard had left Manchester City in May after a decade that produced 20 trophies, including six Premier League titles and the 2022-23 Champions League.

Two obstacles proved insurmountable. Guardiola's reported salary demand of around €20 million per year was roughly double the FIGC's budget, according to La Gazzetta dello Sport. More critically, the 55-year-old has decided to take at least a year away from the dugout to spend time with his family in Barcelona.

Guardiola told the federation he had "seriously considered" the offer but that the timing was wrong, according to La Gazzetta. He still sees himself as a day-to-day training-pitch coach rather than one suited to the part-time rhythm of international management.

Why Pirlo?

With the two marquee names out of contention, attention shifted quickly to Pirlo — a move Maldini reportedly favoured all along as a longer-term appointment. The 47-year-old is a member of Italy's 2006 World Cup-winning squad and a former teammate of both Maldini and Leonardo at AC Milan.

Pirlo's managerial CV is modest. He lifted the Coppa Italia during a single season at Juventus in 2020-21 before moving to Fatih Karagümrük in Turkey and then Sampdoria in Serie B. He joined UAE Pro League side United FC in July 2025, but reports indicate an agreement to terminate that contract will not be an obstacle.

His deal with the FIGC is expected to run until the end of the 2030 World Cup at a salary of approximately €1.5 million per year — a fraction of what Guardiola, Ancelotti, Antonio Conte, or Roberto Mancini would have commanded.

Other Contenders Fall Away

Conte, who managed Italy between 2014 and 2016 and most recently coached Napoli, was reportedly not Maldini's preferred profile. Mancini, who led Italy to the 2021 European Championship title before a controversial departure to Saudi Arabia in 2023, drew interest from Malago but lingering resentment over that exit complicated any return.

"The ideal would be to have the coach by the end of this week, but perhaps even more ideal would be to wait for the person we really want. There is a certain hurry, but not a hasty one."

— Paolo Maldini, FIGC Technical Director

What's Next

The Azzurri face a daunting rebuild. Maldini and Leonardo have warned that returning Italy to the top of international football could take eight to ten years — a timeline that underscores the federation's desire for a coach willing to invest in youth development and a clear playing identity rather than quick fixes.

Pirlo's first major target would be qualification for Euro 2028 in the United Kingdom and Ireland, a tournament Italy will need to reach through the qualifying rounds after their World Cup humiliation. If confirmed, he will inherit a squad stripped of several veteran players who retired internationally after the qualifying failure.

For now, the FIGC appears ready to bet on one of its greatest-ever players to write a new chapter for the Azzurri — even if his coaching pedigree does not yet match his legend on the pitch.
